title: As to a friend
hookLine: Kristin Neff's research on self-compassion: kindness to yourself, shared humanity, mindfulness
carry: what would I say to a friend

lines: YOU'D NEVER TALK TO HER LIKE THAT.
cards: Your friend calls. She forgot an important meeting, her boss was annoyed, and she feels like an idiot. What do you say?
Probably: that's awful, but it happens to everyone, you're not an idiot, what do you need? Now you forgot the meeting. Listen to what Brewer calls the chatter.
Idiot. Always like this. Everyone saw.

Said to a friend, those words would end the friendship. In the early 2000s a psychologist named Kristin Neff started studying what happens when people take the voice they use for a friend and point it inward.

teach.b: Neff described self-compassion in three parts, each set against its opposite.
First, kindness to yourself instead of harsh judgment: not pretending the mistake didn't happen, but talking to yourself about it the way a good friend would.
Second, shared humanity instead of isolation. Failing can feel like you're the only one. The room is full: other people forget meetings, lose their temper, lie awake at 2am.

Third, mindfulness instead of getting swept away. You see the pain clearly, without shoving it down and without making it the whole story. Now the obvious objection: if I'm kind to myself, won't I stop trying?
The research points the other way.

In one set of studies at Berkeley, people nudged toward self-compassion after a failure studied longer for a retest, and were more willing to make amends for a past wrong, than people nudged toward self-esteem.

teach.h: KINDNESS MAKES IT SAFER TO LOOK.
teach.b: Kindness seems to make it safer to look at what went wrong. A caution: much of this research is correlation and short experiments. Encouraging, not a miracle.
In the Pali texts, King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika admit to each other that no one is dearer to them than themselves. The Buddha doesn't scold them.
He says that searching in every direction you find no one dearer than yourself, and since everyone feels this way, whoever cares for themselves should not harm another.
Self-regard, in that telling, is where regard for others starts.

how: In self-compassion practice, developed from Kristin Neff's research, people notice their pain, remind themselves others go through the same, and speak to themselves as they would to a friend.

o: the psychologist who mapped self-compassion's three parts
a researcher who showed self-esteem beats self-kindness
the monk who first taught loving-kindness meditation

games.q: Neff's three parts — tap the pairs.

s: being kind to yourself makes you lazy
in studies, self-compassion after failure led people to study longer, not less.
self-compassion means pretending the mistake didn't happen
it means seeing it clearly and responding the way a good friend would.
in a Pali text, the Buddha links caring for yourself to not harming others
no one is dearer than oneself; since all feel this, one should not harm another.

games.q: you snap at your kid and feel terrible. the inner voice says: you're a bad parent. what does self-compassion suggest?
o: agree with the voice: you deserve it.
say what you'd say to a friend, and make amends.
games.why: kindness, shared humanity, clear seeing: other parents snap too. studies found self-compassion made people more willing to make amends.

practice: Think of one thing you've been hard on yourself about lately, hear what your inner voice says about it, then imagine a friend telling you that exact story about themselves.
Silently say to yourself what you'd say back to them, even if it feels awkward. Then add one line: other people have done this too.

wordCard.voice: Neff, who named self-compassion's three parts, kindness, shared humanity and mindfulness: the voice you'd use for a friend, turned inward.

carryVoice: Your line: what would I say to a friend. The kind voice was yours all along. Day three hundred fourteen, done.
